title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count things, say and ask ages and phone numbers, use 'first, second, third…' and talk about amounts.
intro:
Hindi numbers from 1 to 100 are famously irregular — every one is its own word (look at the numbers chart in the course overview and learn them in tens). The good news: in shops and on phones, people constantly switch to English numbers, so you can get by while you learn.

In this unit you'll use numbers in sentences: how many, how much, how old, and which (first, second…).

m · pl unchanged · formal: वर्ष varṣ
ढाई सौ 250. From 3½ on, use साढ़े (Unit 7).

grammar.title: Counting nouns and asking 'how many / how much'
grammar.body:
After **एक** 'one' the noun is singular; after any other number it is plural: एक लड़का, दो लड़के; एक लड़की, दो लड़कियाँ. (Masculine nouns not ending in -ā look the same: एक आदमी, दस आदमी.)

**कितना** 'how much / how many' is an adjective, so it agrees with the noun:

**कितना** + m. singular (uncountable): कितना पानी? 'how much water?'
**कितनी** + feminine: कितनी किताबें? 'how many books?', कितनी चीनी? 'how much sugar?'
**कितने** + m. plural: कितने लोग? 'how many people?'

**दोनों** 'both' and **तीनों** 'all three' follow the noun or pronoun: हम दोनों 'both of us'. **डेढ़** 1½ and **ढाई** 2½ are everyday numbers, used for kilos, hours and prices.

examples.en: one and a half kilos of potatoes
The three of us are brothers.

grammar.title: Age and ordinals
grammar.body:
To give your age, Hindi says 'I am 25 years **of**': **मैं पच्चीस साल का हूँ** — and का agrees with **you**: का for a male, की for a female, के for a respected person or a group. The question is **आप कितने साल के हैं?** (or की for a woman), or simply **आपकी उम्र क्या है?**

**Ordinals** are adjectives ending in -ā, so they change for gender and number like अच्छा: पहला / पहली / पहले. From 'fifth' on, add **-वाँ** (m), **-वीं** (f), **-वें** (pl) to the number: पाँचवाँ, बीसवीं, सौवें. The irregular ones are पहला, दूसरा, तीसरा, चौथा and छठा.

examples.native: मेरी दादी अस्सी साल की हैं।
examples.roman: merī dādī assī sāl kī haiṃ.

dialogue.title: Checking in at a yoga retreat
dialogue.setting: Tom arrives at a retreat in Rishikesh and fills in the register with the man at the desk.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: नौ आठ सात छह, पाँच चार, तीन दो एक शून्य।
lines.roman: nau āṭh sāt chhah, pāṃch chār, tīn do ek shūnya.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: हम दो लोग हैं — मैं और मेरी पत्नी।
lines.roman: ham do log haiṃ — maiṃ aur merī patnī.
lines.en: Two of us — me and my wife.

lines.speaker: Clerk
lines.native: ठीक है। आपका कमरा पहली मंज़िल पर है, कमरा नंबर एक सौ बारह।
lines.roman: ṭhīk hai. āpkā kamrā pahlī manzil par hai, kamrā nambar ek sau bārah.
lines.en: OK. Your room is on the first floor, room number 112.

culture: Indians count large numbers in **lakhs** (1,00,000) and **crores** (1,00,00,000), and commas are placed accordingly — you'll see prices like ₹1,50,000 (डेढ़ लाख). In everyday life, phone numbers, prices and times are very often said in English, especially in cities. Fractions are used constantly: डेढ़ (1½), ढाई (2½), and साढ़े '…and a half' (साढ़े तीन 3½). Ages are asked freely, and older people are addressed with respect — never comment that an elder looks 'old' as a compliment… unless you mean wise!
